title: Recruiting SaaS Trains Your Replacement
existing_summary: Handshake, originally a recruiting platform, is now offering professionals up to $30,000 for work documents that can train AI systems. The shift is hard to miss: a marketplace built to connect companies with human talent is starting to monetize the work itself. If that continues, recruiting platforms may eventually stop supplying workers and start supplying AI trained on them.

title: Tesco Lets AI Build the Basket
existing_summary: Tesco is testing an AI meal-planning assistant that uses preferences and dietary needs to recommend recipes and add ingredients directly to shoppers' baskets. Backed by decades of Clubcard data, the system shifts retail competition from physical shelf space toward algorithmic selection. For brands, being chosen by the AI may increasingly matter more than winning prominent placement in-store.
summary_bullets: Tesco testing AI meal-planning assistant with recipe recommendations
System uses decades of Clubcard data to personalize suggestions
Shifts retail competition from shelf placement to algorithmic selection
full_text:
# Brands Are Losing Shelf Space to AI Algorithms

By [PYMNTS](https://www.pymnts.com/author/pymnts/)  |  August 18, 2026

[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https://www.pymnts.com/news/retail/2026/brands-are-losing-shelf-space-to-ai-algorithms/&t=Brands+Are+Losing+Shelf+Space+to+AI+Algorithms "Share on Facebook")[](<https://twitter.com/share?text=Brands+Are+Losing+Shelf+Space+to+AI+Algorithms                        -&url=https://www.pymnts.com/news/retail/2026/brands-are-losing-shelf-space-to-ai-algorithms/> "Tweet This Post")[](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https://www.pymnts.com/news/retail/2026/brands-are-losing-shelf-space-to-ai-algorithms/&title=Brands+Are+Losing+Shelf+Space+to+AI+Algorithms&summary=&source= "Share on LinkedIn")[](<mailto:?subject=Brands Are Losing Shelf Space to AI Algorithms&BODY=I found this article interesting and want to share it with you. Check it out: https://www.pymnts.com/news/retail/2026/brands-are-losing-shelf-space-to-ai-algorithms/> "Share via Email") |  Listen to Article Listen Pause

![Tesco AI shopping](https://www.pymnts.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Tesco-AI-shopping-1.jpg?w=620)

Tesco has spent three decades learning what more than 24 million U.K. households buy through its Clubcard loyalty program. Now the grocer is testing what happens when artificial intelligence stops recommending groceries and starts building the basket itself.

## Get the Full Story

Complete the form to unlock this article and enjoy unlimited free access to all PYMNTS content — no additional logins required.

 

yesSubscribe to our daily newsletter, PYMNTS Today.

By completing this form, you agree to receive marketing communications from PYMNTS and to the sharing of your information with our sponsor, if applicable, in accordance with our [Privacy Policy](https://pymnts-com-develop.go-vip.net/privacy-policy/) and [Terms and Conditions](https://pymnts-com-develop.go-vip.net/terms-conditions/).

Δ

Tesco’s pilot is a meal-planning assistant, built with U.K. AI consultancy [Tomoro](https://tomoronow.com/), that suggests recipe ideas based on a customer’s preferences and dietary needs and can add the recommended ingredients directly into a shopper’s basket, [Retail Gazette reported](https://www.retailgazette.co.uk/blog/2026/04/tesco-trials-ai-shopping-assistant-with-280000-colleagues-ahead-of-customer-rollout/). The assistant is in beta with roughly 280,000 Tesco employees ahead of a wider customer rollout, Retail Gazette also reported.

That Tomoro-built tool runs separately from Tesco’s other AI bets, though the strategy overlaps. Tesco’s strategic partnership with Adobe, announced in April, brings agentic AI capabilities and personalized content generation to Clubcard offers and marketing rather than to the meal planner itself, [Adobe said](https://news.adobe.com/en/gb/news/2026/04/adobe-tesco-enter-strategic-ai-partnership) in the announcement. The two companies also launched a joint Innovation Lab, embedding Adobe engineers alongside Tesco’s technology teams.

Tesco controls close to 30% of the U.K. grocery market, and Clubcard remains one of retail’s largest first-party datasets: purchasing histories stretching back three decades, [according to Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/bernardmarr/2026/08/12/tescos-ai-agents-could-soon-do-your-shopping-for-you/) contributor Bernard Marr.

“Few retailers anywhere in the world have built the depth of trust and knowledge that Tesco has,” [Nathan Hancock](https://www.linkedin.com/in/nathanhancock/), Adobe’s vice president and managing director for the U.K., Ireland, Middle East and Africa, [told](https://www.thegrocer.co.uk/news/tesco-and-adobe-sign-ai-deal-to-boost-clubcard-personalisation/717628.article) The Grocer, calling the combination “a genuine step-change for modern retail personalization.”

Tesco separately [signed](https://www.tescoplc.com/tesco-and-mistral-ai-sign-new-generative-ai-agreement/) a three-year agreement with AI company Mistral in December covering internal workflows and a Clubcard offers overhaul, the third piece of an AI strategy that now touches meal planning, marketing and back-end operations at once.

## Retailers Are Racing to Own the Meal Decision Before the List Exists

Tesco is not the only one. Albertsons’ Ask AI search tool, launched last September, delivered a 10% increase in basket size for customers using it, CEO [Susan Morris](https://www.linkedin.com/in/morris-susan/) said on the company’s January earnings call, [PYMNTS reported](https://www.pymnts.com/news/artificial-intelligence/2026/albertsons-says-ai-shopping-assistant-increased-customers-basket-size-10percent/). The company also rolled out a more comprehensive agentic shopping assistant across all its store banners in December.

The shared logic across retailers testing this approach is that whoever answers a customer’s “What’s for dinner?” question first gets to decide what ends up in the cart, rather than losing that decision to a recipe website or a rival retailer’s app.

“The ability to actively shape demand and influence which products end up in baskets at scale” is what makes agentic AI — AI that acts on a shopper’s behalf rather than simply generating suggestions — different from a standard recommendation engine, said [Gabriel Corbett](https://www.linkedin.com/in/gabrielcorbett/), co-founder and CEO of [Mealia](https://mealia.com/us/home), a U.K.-based AI grocery app integrated with Tesco, Asda, Sainsbury’s and Morrisons, in an interview with  [The Grocer](https://www.thegrocer.co.uk/news/ai-grocery-app-helping-supermarkets-win-back-share-from-meal-kit-providers/712941.article). The same model lets retailers steer demand toward at-risk inventory, improving margins while cutting food waste.

Consumer appetite for that shift is measurable: 69% of consumers say they are interested in delegating subscription management, grocery shopping and meal planning to agentic AI, [according to PYMNTS Intelligence’](https://www.pymnts.com/news/artificial-intelligence/2026/70-percent-of-consumers-say-yes-to-ai-agents-for-shopping/)s survey of 2,299 U.S. adults tracking interest across 54 personal AI use cases. The survey reflects U.S. shoppers rather than Tesco’s U.K. customer base, but the appetite it captures lines up with what retailers on both sides of the Atlantic are now building toward. That figure sits among the highest of any category tested, alongside health and wellness management and travel planning, suggesting grocery shopping, a repetitive task with a limited, predictable product set, is one of the categories consumers are most ready to hand off.

## Shelf Space Is Becoming a Spot in the Algorithm

That shift has a direct consequence for brands that have spent decades competing for physical shelf placement and in-store promotion. If an AI assistant reconstructs a customer’s weekly shop automatically from stored preferences, a brand not already part of that customer’s established pattern may never get surfaced for consideration, regardless of how much a retailer would normally charge for prominent placement. Retail media budgets built around influencing a shopper browsing a page may need to shift toward influencing the data and rules an AI agent weighs before a shopping list is ever generated.

For Tesco specifically, the test is whether three decades of Clubcard data is detailed enough to make that automated basket genuinely useful rather than simply convenient. A customer whose weekly shop gets reconstructed accurately has less reason to browse, compare or switch retailers at all, precisely the kind of habitual, low-friction purchasing loop every major grocery chain testing this technology is now racing to build first.

title: Visa and Mastercard Join Agentic Alliance

# Visa and Mastercard Join Rain’s Agentic Commerce Coalition

By [PYMNTS](https://www.pymnts.com/author/pymnts/)  |  August 18, 2026

[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https://www.pymnts.com/news/artificial-intelligence/2026/visa-and-mastercard-join-rains-agentic-commerce-coalition/&t=Visa+and+Mastercard+Join+Rain%E2%80%99s+Agentic+Commerce+Coalition "Share on Facebook")[](<https://twitter.com/share?text=Visa+and+Mastercard+Join+Rain%E2%80%99s+Agentic+Commerce+Coalition                        -&url=https://www.pymnts.com/news/artificial-intelligence/2026/visa-and-mastercard-join-rains-agentic-commerce-coalition/> "Tweet This Post")[](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https://www.pymnts.com/news/artificial-intelligence/2026/visa-and-mastercard-join-rains-agentic-commerce-coalition/&title=Visa+and+Mastercard+Join+Rain%E2%80%99s+Agentic+Commerce+Coalition&summary=&source= "Share on LinkedIn")[](<mailto:?subject=Visa and Mastercard Join Rain’s Agentic Commerce Coalition&BODY=I found this article interesting and want to share it with you. Check it out: https://www.pymnts.com/news/artificial-intelligence/2026/visa-and-mastercard-join-rains-agentic-commerce-coalition/> "Share via Email") |  Listen to Article Listen Pause

![](https://www.pymnts.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/AI-agentic-shopping-buy-with-AI1.jpg?w=620)

Stablecoin payments infrastructure company [Rain](https://www.rain.xyz/) has formed a group to promote agentic commerce development.

## Get the Full Story

Complete the form to unlock this article and enjoy unlimited free access to all PYMNTS content — no additional logins required.

 

yesSubscribe to our daily newsletter, PYMNTS Today.

By completing this form, you agree to receive marketing communications from PYMNTS and to the sharing of your information with our sponsor, if applicable, in accordance with our [Privacy Policy](https://pymnts-com-develop.go-vip.net/privacy-policy/) and [Terms and Conditions](https://pymnts-com-develop.go-vip.net/terms-conditions/).

Δ

The Agentic Payments Alliance (APA) was [announced](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/rain-launches-the-agentic-payments-alliance-to-guide-the-future-of-agent-driven-commerce-302853532.html) Tuesday (Aug. 18), listing [Visa](https://www.visa.com/en-us), [Mastercard](https://www.mastercard.com/us/en.html), [Fiserv](https://www.fiserv.com/en.html), [Circle](https://circle.so/), [Solana](https://solana.com/) and [Remitly](https://www.remitly.com/) among its founding members.

“No single company should get to decide how agents transact on someone’s behalf. That has to come from the platforms building the rails, the regulators setting the rules, and the innovators closest to how agents are actually being used today,” Farooq Malik, co-founder and CEO of Rain, said in a news release.

“We initiated the Agentic Payments Alliance to put all of these parties in the same room, and to do it now, while the category is still taking shape.”

The release cites projections from McKinsey estimating between $3 trillion and $5 trillion in global agentic AI commerce by 2030.

What’s still being defined, Rain said, is the infrastructure that allows that activity: how artificial intelligence agents are authorized, how [fraud is detected](https://www.pymnts.com/cybersecurity/fraud-prevention/2026/agentic-agents-confront-and-combat-fraud-as-scams-accelerate/), and how loyalty and rewards will work. The company said it formed the APA to “bring the people building that infrastructure into the same conversation, before those decisions get made in isolation.”

Rain says it has spent the last year “building toward this moment,” with [offerings](https://www.pymnts.com/news/loyalty-and-rewards-news/2026/rain-debuts-native-loyalty-stablecoin-card-programs/) like including its Agent Control Layer and Scoped Cards, which provide agents with widely accepted payment credentials “that are safe and limited.”

“That work put Rain in a position to convene founding members across the industry rather than build the category alone,” the release said. “The Alliance itself is a working coalition, run collectively by its founding members rather than owned by any one company. Members will set its charter and mission together.”

The group’s early work is expected to involve shared research and frameworks, experimenting with emerging standards for AI agent identity and authorization, and advocating on the regulatory questions raised by agentic commerce, Rain said.

PYMNTS [wrote](https://www.pymnts.com/credit-cards/2026/cards-make-their-case-in-an-agentic-world/) earlier this month about how Visa, Mastercard and fellow card giants [American Express](https://www.americanexpress.com/) and [Capital One](https://www.capitalone.com/) are developing “the rails” for agentic commerce.

“Agentic commerce is a when, not an if,” Visa CEO [Ryan McInerney](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ryan-mcinerney-79838697) said during an earnings call. “We’re building the products, the services, the protocols, ensuring that the ecosystem has what it takes, and this will happen, and it will be a positive tailwind for Visa.”

title: AI Can Recommend, But Who Pays?
existing_summary: PYMNTS found 61% of U.S. consumers would consider Pay Later financing recommended by AI, provided they retain final approval and receive clear cost and credit protections. But the survey leaves a bigger question unanswered: if an AI recommends a bad financing option and the consumer loses money, it never addresses who ultimately bears responsibility for that decision.
summary_bullets: 61% of U.S. consumers open to AI-recommended Pay Later financing
Consumers want final approval and clear cost/credit protections
Unresolved question of liability if AI recommends bad financing options

# 61% of Consumers Would Consider AI-Recommended Financing

By [PYMNTS](https://www.pymnts.com/author/pymnts/)  |  August 18, 2026

[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https://www.pymnts.com/consumer-insights/2026/61percent-of-consumers-would-consider-ai-recommended-financing/&t=61%25+of+Consumers+Would+Consider+AI-Recommended+Financing "Share on Facebook")[](<https://twitter.com/share?text=61%25+of+Consumers+Would+Consider+AI-Recommended+Financing                        -&url=https://www.pymnts.com/consumer-insights/2026/61percent-of-consumers-would-consider-ai-recommended-financing/> "Tweet This Post")[](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https://www.pymnts.com/consumer-insights/2026/61percent-of-consumers-would-consider-ai-recommended-financing/&title=61%25+of+Consumers+Would+Consider+AI-Recommended+Financing&summary=&source= "Share on LinkedIn")[](<mailto:?subject=61% of Consumers Would Consider AI-Recommended Financing&BODY=I found this article interesting and want to share it with you. Check it out: https://www.pymnts.com/consumer-insights/2026/61percent-of-consumers-would-consider-ai-recommended-financing/> "Share via Email") |  Listen to Article Listen Pause

![graphic on AI pay later](https://www.pymnts.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/AI-pay-later-data-brief.png?w=620)

Artificial intelligence may win a place at the Pay Later checkout by recommending the financing, then letting the shopper make the final call. New PYMNTS Intelligence data shows 61% of U.S. consumers would consider an AI shopping assistant’s Pay Later recommendation for at least one common purchase category.

## Get the Full Story

Complete the form to unlock this article and enjoy unlimited free access to all PYMNTS content — no additional logins required.

 

yesSubscribe to our daily newsletter, PYMNTS Today.

By completing this form, you agree to receive marketing communications from PYMNTS and to the sharing of your information with our sponsor, if applicable, in accordance with our [Privacy Policy](https://pymnts-com-develop.go-vip.net/privacy-policy/) and [Terms and Conditions](https://pymnts-com-develop.go-vip.net/terms-conditions/).

Δ

The June 2026 edition of The Pay Later Ecosystem Report, titled “[Consumers Will Let AI Recommend Pay Later, But They Want Control](https://www.pymnts.com/study/pay-later-ecosystem-consumers-want-ai-recommendations-control/),” draws on a survey of 2,034 U.S. adults. It found 39% of the surveyed consumers had used AI for a payment-related activity during the previous three months. Consumers also showed broader interest in using AI to compare Pay Later choices, provided the technology protects their credit, keeps costs down and asks permission before completing a purchase.

## **Key Points:**

*   Interest extends beyond young adults. Gen Z leads, with 80% open to an AI-recommended Pay Later option in at least one category. Millennials follow at 78% and bridge millennials at 69%. The notable figure is Gen X: 60% are open to the idea. Baby boomers show less interest, with 36% expressing interest. That reach suggests providers can design for a wider market instead of treating the service as a youth feature.
*   Electronics offers the clearest opening. Seventeen percent of consumers would let AI recommend a Pay Later option for electronics. Furniture, apparel, travel and everyday essentials each drew 13%. Home services or repairs followed at 12%, while medical or dental expenses and auto-related costs each reached 11%. Consumers appear willing to seek help with both planned purchases and bills that arrive unexpectedly.
*   Control can turn interest into use. Among the conditions consumers selected, choosing the most affordable option and requiring approval before a plan is finalized tied for first at 24% each. Avoiding a new account or credit application and setting a maximum purchase amount followed at 21% each. Only 2% would let AI decide without limits. The preferred model looks like a knowledgeable store clerk who explains the choices, then waits for the customer to sign.

Other findings reinforce that practical approach. Fifty-nine percent rated protection from harm to their credit score as very or extremely important. Fifty-six percent prioritized the lowest total cost over time and 54% wanted the most affordable monthly payment. Approval before purchase was also the leading trust builder at 28%, followed by confirmation of total cost at 25%.

The report points toward an encouraging path for the Pay Later ecosystem: AI can make financing easier to compare while consumers retain authority over the final decision.

title: AI Makes Human Stories More Valuable
existing_summary: Entrepreneur contributor Jonny Caplan argues that as AI floods media with cheap, instantly generated content, authentic human storytelling will become more valuable. Audiences increasingly have unlimited content but limited trust and attention, making emotion, judgment and genuine experience harder to replicate. For media companies and brands, the advantage shifts from producing more content to creating stories people actually care about.
summary_bullets: AI-generated content flooding media increases value of authentic human storytelling
Audiences have unlimited content but limited trust and attention
Advantage shifts to creating stories people care about rather than volume
full_text:
# Why Authentic Storytelling Is Becoming Media’s Most Valuable Asset

In an age of endless content, audiences are now searching for stories that provide meaning, authenticity and genuine human connection.

## Key Takeaways

*   Audiences have endless content but limited time, trust and emotional energy.
*   Human stories make factual content powerful: Documentaries, sports, technology and business become compelling when they reveal the people, emotions and stakes behind the subject.  
    

For much of the last decade, the media industry has been engaged in a relentless [race for attention](https://www.entrepreneur.com/living/how-to-build-your-attention-span/395802). More platforms. More content. More notifications. More algorithms. More opportunities to consume information at every waking moment.

We have created extraordinary access, but also an environment in which almost everything competes for attention and very little is truly understood. The problem is no longer a shortage of content. It is a shortage of meaning.

Despite being more digitally connected than ever, many people feel less personally connected. Social media allows us to communicate instantly across continents, yet much of that communication has been reduced to fleeting validation and carefully curated identities.

We know what people are doing, where they are travelling and what they have achieved. We do not necessarily know what they have overcome or who they really are. Against a backdrop of geopolitical uncertainty, economic volatility, rapid technological disruption and growing social division, audiences are looking for understanding.

## The real battle is not for attention

Deloitte’s 2026 Digital Media Trends [report](https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/insights/industry/technology/digital-media-trends-consumption-habits-survey.html) found that the average consumer spends around six hours each day on media and entertainment, while 41% had canceled a streaming subscription during the previous six months. This does not suggest people have stopped consuming content. It shows how brutally competitive the fight to remain relevant has become.

Audiences have almost unlimited choice, but their time, trust and emotional energy remain limited.

The question facing every broadcaster, platform, producer and brand is no longer simply: Can we get someone to press play? It is: Can we make them care enough to continue?

An [algorithm](https://www.entrepreneur.com/growing-a-business/how-to-keep-your-marketing-human-in-an-algorithm-driven/501949?itm_campaign=wp-parsely&itm_medium=smart-link&itm_term=ed68edc1471a20d456ac524bc12d4bd2&itm_source=smart-linking "Data Is Only Half the Story When It Comes to Marketing — Here’s How to Balance It With Real Human Emotion") may place content in front of millions of people, but distribution alone does not create a connection. A view is not a relationship. A click is not trust. A moment of attention is not necessarily a memory.

Meaningful storytelling begins where the metric ends.

## Why factual stories are finding new relevance

This is one reason factual content remains so powerful.

Documentaries, docudramas, biographies and real-world storytelling offer something much of the media landscape struggles to manufacture: authenticity. At their best, they do not simply explain what happened. They reveal why it mattered.

A documentary about artificial intelligence is rarely compelling because of the [technology alone](https://www.entrepreneur.com/science-technology/tech-alone-wont-shape-the-future-heres-why-we-need/498323?itm_campaign=wp-parsely&itm_medium=smart-link&itm_term=232f318828f750121fcdc4ce0231d30b&itm_source=smart-linking "Tech Alone Won’t Shape the Future — Here’s Why We Need Human Influence"). It becomes compelling when we meet the scientist attempting to build it, the entrepreneur risking everything on it, the worker whose role may disappear because of it and the family wondering what it will mean for the next generation.

A program about space is not really about rockets. It is about ambition, fear, sacrifice and humanity’s desire to discover what lies beyond the horizon.

A business story is not ultimately about valuations or balance sheets. It is about belief, risk, betrayal, resilience and the people who continue building when everybody else thinks they should stop. Information tells us what happened. [Storytelling makes us care](https://www.entrepreneur.com/starting-a-business/how-brands-can-use-authenticity-and-emotional-connection-to/447762?itm_campaign=wp-parsely&itm_medium=smart-link&itm_term=51a029abaf76312270fba5aaf99d07d7&itm_source=smart-linking "Digital Storytelling: How Brands Can Use Authenticity and Emotional Connection to Stand Out Online").

Formula One is a strong example. The sport already had speed, danger, glamour and global competition. Netflix’s _Drive to Survive_ translated that world into characters, rivalries, vulnerability and emotional stakes.

Formula One’s 2025 Global Fan Survey [showed](https://www.formula1.com/en/latest/article/formula-1-and-motorsport-network-unveil-2025-global-fan-survey.4YqMebNy8BLaapyJfjzDXO) the sport attracting a younger and increasingly female audience, with women accounting for three in four new fans. The series did not merely document an existing audience. It helped make an established sport emotionally accessible to a new one.

That is the power of factual storytelling. It can take something technical, unfamiliar or apparently niche and make it matter to millions.

## Brands are learning the same lesson

Interruption-based advertising is losing its effectiveness. Consumers have learned to spot content that feels transactional, and they scroll past it, skip it, mute it, block it, or unsubscribe. The strongest brands are no longer focused only on how to promote a product. They are asking which stories they have the credibility to tell.

Red Bull is a leading example. It has built a global media business around sports, culture, adventure, and human achievement. People can choose to watch its content without any immediate interest in buying an energy drink.

The content delivers value first. The brand association follows.

Red Bull Media House produces and licenses live events, short- and long-form programming, and feature films across television, mobile, digital, audio, and print. It has grown beyond advertising into a legitimate international media operation.

That is very different from repackaging a commercial as entertainment.

Branded storytelling works only when the audience matters more than the message. The story needs truth, tension, independence, and genuine human interest. If the marketing department has already written the conclusion, audiences will notice.

Authenticity is what matters most. A brand cannot buy trust simply by attaching itself to an important issue. It earns trust by adding something useful, credible, and open-minded to the conversation.

## Artificial intelligence will make meaning more valuable

AI will change how content is researched, created, translated and distributed. It will make production faster and put [advanced creative tools](https://www.entrepreneur.com/growing-a-business/ai-made-the-internet-louder-than-ever-heres-how-to-use/484127?itm_campaign=wp-parsely&itm_medium=smart-link&itm_term=e54f8b8885881dc2545a3f3cc19d9a94&itm_source=smart-linking "AI Made the Internet Louder Than Ever — Here’s How to Use It to Cut Through the Noise and Make a Lasting Impact") in more hands than ever before. It will also flood the world with [instantly generated content](https://www.entrepreneur.com/growing-a-business/ai-video-has-changed-marketing-forever-heres-how-to-adapt/497898?itm_campaign=wp-parsely&itm_medium=smart-link&itm_term=d1cdf3ab5592c54845a3600982b78aba&itm_source=smart-linking "AI Video Has Changed Marketing Forever — and Standing Out Requires a New Strategy").

That will not make human storytellers less important. It will make them essential.

When content is easy to produce, meaning becomes harder to find. AI can process information at remarkable speed, but strong storytelling still depends on imagination, judgment, empathy, and curiosity.

In my work covering technology, entrepreneurship, AI and space, I have found that the innovation itself is rarely the full story. What people remember is the human experience behind it: the inventor dismissed early on, the founder who rebuilt after failure, or the family affected by a major technological decision.

Technology creates the setting. Humanity creates the story.

## Creating content that matters

The media industry has spent years attempting to create more content, distribute it faster and target it more precisely. But audiences do not have a [relationship with volume](https://www.entrepreneur.com/growing-a-business/how-to-navigate-brand-authenticity-in-the-age-of-ai-slop/503454?itm_campaign=wp-parsely&itm_medium=smart-link&itm_term=9def2f064c7e873c76c5597c03805c10&itm_source=smart-linking "How to Create Brand Authenticity in the Age of AI Slop").

They have relationships with characters, ideas and emotions. They remember the story that changed their perspective, introduced them to a world they had never seen or made them feel less alone.

An advertising campaign often ends when the media budget ends. A powerful story can travel across broadcasters, [streaming platforms](https://www.entrepreneur.com/science-technology/why-the-entertainment-and-social-media-industries-are/376241?itm_campaign=wp-parsely&itm_medium=smart-link&itm_term=adccba71e389c96a8a0bf86a06cb53f2&itm_source=smart-linking "Why the Entertainment and Social Media Industries are Converging"), social media and territories for years, reaching entirely new audiences.

For all the advances in artificial intelligence, streaming technology and global distribution, the underlying human need that drives storytelling remains remarkably consistent.

People want to understand themselves. They want to understand others. They want to understand the world in which they live.

They want to [feel connected](https://www.entrepreneur.com/growing-a-business/chasing-social-media-algorithms-is-out-community-is-in/473217?itm_campaign=wp-parsely&itm_medium=smart-link&itm_term=f26ea90fdfed2e8ff1d5d6552c59bcdb&itm_source=smart-linking "Chasing Social Media Algorithms Is Out — Community Is in. Here’s How to Create Connections That Matter.").
